title: The Pleasure of Knowing What’s for Lunch
angle: A familiar meal can comfort not because it is special, but because repetition lets attention settle into its small pleasures.
paragraphs: A familiar lunch has a quiet advantage: it doesn’t require a meeting about itself. The bread is in the same cupboard, the cheese is the same kind, and there is no menu to study or recipe to interpret. You can make the sandwich while thinking about something else, then notice the crisp edge of the toast only when you sit down.

Novelty gets plenty of attention, but repetition has its own texture. When you already know what a meal will taste like, there is less suspense to manage. The pleasure can be small and exact: a ripe pear after something salty, soup warm enough to take slowly, the last bite that catches the bit of mustard you missed at first. Nothing needs to be transformed into an occasion.

Of course, the same lunch every day could become dull, and sometimes the cupboard offers a persuasive argument for trying something different. But not every ordinary pleasure needs a surprise attached. A meal can be good partly because it asks so little of the afternoon. Then the plate is empty, the kitchen is still the kitchen, and the day carries on without a review of the experience.
